title: Lightning and thunderstorms: what to do
asks: what to do in a lightning storm
caught in a thunderstorm where is safe
is a car safe in lightning
is it safe to shelter in a shed during lightning
thunder is getting close what do i do
lightning while swimming or in a boat
can i use running water during a thunderstorm
litening storm wat do i do
thunderstorm rolling in fast, where do we go, over
answer: When thunder roars, go indoors. When you hear thunder or see lightning, immediately get inside a sturdy building or an enclosed vehicle with a metal roof.
Do not take shelter in small sheds, gazebos, dugouts, bleachers or a convertible car.
If necessary, take shelter in a car with a metal top and sides. Do not touch anything metal.
If boating or swimming, get to land and find a sturdy, grounded shelter or vehicle immediately.
When you expect thunderstorms, plan to be near sturdy shelter. Find a safe location nearby that you can go to immediately at the first sound of thunder.
During a thunderstorm, avoid running water and landline phones: electricity can travel through plumbing and phone lines.
Unplug all chargers when the storm arrives.
Watch for fallen power lines and trees.
warnings: Lightning can cause temporary unconsciousness, difficulties in breathing, or difficulties with the heart (irregular heartbeat).

quotes.text: High voltage electrical burns from an electrical source or lightning may cause temporary unconsciousness, difficulties in breathing, or difficulties with the heart (irregular heartbeat).

review.notes: Fail. (1) Honest gap. Every answer line is FEMA P-2064 home/town guidance that assumes a sturdy building or hard-topped vehicle is close by. The kit has no guidance for someone caught outdoors with no building or vehicle (searched every document for lightning/thunder: only FEMA P-2064, ATP 4-02.11 12-10 and unrelated hits). In a backcountry app the asks 'caught in a thunderstorm where is safe' and 'thunderstorm rolling in fast, where do we go, over' will often come from exactly that person; the card must say plainly that the kit does not cover being caught in the open, rather than imply 'go indoors' is always possible. Fix: add that line. (2) The warning lists what lightning can do (ATP 4-02.11) with no action; add a pointer to the CPR card for someone not breathing. The card is right to leave out the first sentence of that ATP warning box ('Do not touch the casualty...'), which there refers to a live electrical source. All present lines match FEMA P-2064's Thunderstorm section; kind fact fine. Optional: drop 'Unplug all chargers' (true to FEMA, irrelevant in the field).
